segments.title: The Fog and the Law: Bleak House Opens

utterances.text: Welcome to Bleak House Unpacked — a close, unhurried reading of one of the great novels in the English language.
I'm your host, and over the course of this series we'll be working through Dickens's extraordinary novel chapter by chapter, passage by passage.
We'll be asking what makes it work — not just as social document or Victorian monument, but as a living, breathing piece of storytelling.
Joining me today are three voices I trust completely to do justice to this novel.
Dr. Eleanor Hartley is a novelist and creative writing teacher who is perhaps the finest living reader of how fiction is actually constructed — sentence by sentence, choice by choice.
She has an almost architectural eye for the decisions a writer makes, and Bleak House is a building she knows intimately.
Sir Edmund Leigh is a retired Oxford don and one of the most elegantly contrarian literary minds I know.
Edmund reads novels as moral drama — stories of individual character tested to its limits — and he is beautifully resistant to any reading that reduces fiction to sociology.
And Oliver Trevelyan has read more great novels aloud than anyone alive.
He is an actor, a writer, and a performer who hears Dickens the way a conductor hears a score — every rhythm, every rest, every comic and tragic note.
Today we begin at the beginning — or rather, at the very atmosphere of beginning — with the fog, the court, and the first intimations of what this novel intends to do.
What strikes me immediately, coming back to the opening passages, is how deliberate the darkness is.
Dickens isn't merely setting a scene — he's constructing a moral atmosphere so thick you almost can't breathe inside it.
And it persists. It never quite lifts.
There's a passage late in the novel — after Nemo's death — that I keep returning to, because it crystallises everything Dickens is doing with light and darkness in this book.
The scene ends with the body lying watched in the dark, and Dickens asks — with real anguish — about the woman who once loved this man:
That rhetorical question is doing extraordinary work — it's a cry of grief, but it's also an indictment.
This man has died unidentified, unloved, above ground — and the novel demands we feel the full weight of that.
Eleanor is right that there is grief there — genuine grief, not mere sentiment.
But I'd resist the word indictment, slightly.
What Dickens is doing in that passage is something older and more universal than social criticism.
He is asking what becomes of a human soul when it passes through the world without being truly known.
That is a theological question as much as a political one — and Dickens, for all his reforming energy, always keeps one foot in that older tradition.
Notice the image of the child at the breast — the mother's face, the soft hand.
Dickens writes:
That is not sociology. That is elegy.
Edmund, I hear you — and the elegy is real.
But I have to say, when I read Bleak House aloud, what I feel most keenly is the sheer theatrical machinery of it.
Dickens is always staging effects — and sometimes those effects are devastatingly quiet.
The jingling piano going silent before we settle into grief — that's a performer's instinct, not a philosopher's.
He writes:
That word — rally — is wickedly chosen.
The living rally round their pillows while the dead man lies forgotten. It's comic and appalling at once.
Oliver has put his finger on something I think is central to the whole novel — the way Dickens holds comedy and tragedy in the same hand.
And nowhere is that more visceral than when the novel descends into Tom-all-Alone's.
There's no comedy there — only a kind of horrified moral clarity.
When Bucket leads Snagsby into that street, Dickens piles the senses up until the reader is almost as sickened as the characters.
The parenthetical — 'though the roads are dry elsewhere' — is devastating in its quietness.
It reminds us that this is not weather. This is a choice — a political, economic, human choice — to let some streets drown while others stay dry.
I won't quarrel with the power of that passage — it is genuinely disturbing.
But I am slightly wary of the word 'choice' used so cleanly.
What Dickens captures there is something murkier than a political programme — it is institutional inertia, collective moral failure, the gradual accretion of neglect.
And I think his genius is that poor Snagsby — a decent, timid, thoroughly ordinary man — feels as if he is descending into an infernal gulf.
It is the individual conscience that carries the weight here, not the abstract system.
The infernal gulf — Dickens means that almost literally, doesn't he.
There is something genuinely Dantesque about that descent into Tom-all-Alone's, with Bucket's bull's-eye lamp playing the role of some grim lantern-bearer.
And then the novel pivots — because the darkness doesn't stay in the slums.
It reaches all the way up to Chesney Wold, into the drawing rooms, into the silence between Tulkinghorn and Lady Dedlock.
That scene where he stops her at the door — it's one of the most chilling in the novel.
He doesn't move a muscle. He simply says, with complete calm:
The power in that room is entirely his — and it costs him nothing but the threat.
What I love about that scene structurally is that Tulkinghorn's control is performed through stillness.
The narrator specifies it: he doesn't stir hand or foot or raise his voice.
Dickens writes:
The tripling of negatives — hand, foot, voice — is metrically almost a sentence of imprisonment.
He is utterly, horribly still — and that stillness is the threat.
The fog at the start, the mud in the slums, the terrible stillness in the drawing room — Bleak House builds its world from atmosphere, and atmosphere, in this novel, is never merely decorative.
We'll be returning to all of these threads — the law, the secrets, the suffering, the magnificent grotesquerie of Dickens's London.
Thank you to Eleanor, Edmund, and Oliver for opening up the book so brilliantly — and we'll be back with more shortly.

segments.title: Richard's Gamble: A Young Man Undone

utterances.text: Welcome to Bleak House Unpacked, the programme that takes Dickens's great novel apart, passage by passage, to find out how it actually works.
Today we're looking at one of the novel's most quietly devastating threads: the story of Richard Carstone, a young man with every advantage and no anchor.
With me are three readers who know this novel intimately, each from a very different angle.
Dr. Eleanor Hartley is a novelist and creative-writing teacher whose eye for structural craft I find almost unnervingly sharp.
Sir Edmund Leigh is a retired Oxford don who insists — correctly, I think — that the moral imagination is where Dickens is most serious.
And Oliver Trevelyan has recorded more Dickens audiobooks than any living person, and hears rhythms in the prose the rest of us can only feel.
We begin at the beginning of Richard's story — not the end, which we all know — but that sunlit early chapter when love and hope are still entirely possible.
What strikes me first about Dickens's handling of Richard is how early, and how gently, the warning signs are planted.
We're in Chapter Thirteen, and Richard and Ada have just confided their love to Esther — sitting one on either side of her, which is a lovely, slightly comic image.
And Esther, who is our narrator here, says something that sounds warm but is actually doing real structural work.
She says — and this is her voice — that happiness could come to this love
"only if it were real and lasting and inspired them with a steady resolution to do their duty to each other, with constancy, fortitude, and perseverance, each always for the other's sake."
Constancy. Fortitude. Perseverance. Three words that will become Richard's indictment before the novel is done.
And Dickens makes it almost unbearably sweet in the moment, which is the trick, isn't it?
Richard and Ada are calling Esther all sorts of endearing and sensible names and the three of them sit there advising and talking half the night.
You're entirely charmed. You believe in them completely.
Which is exactly why the next passage — the visual passage, the one with the sunlight — hits with such force.
Dickens writes the young couple leaving the room, and Esther and Mr. Jarndyce watch them go.

"So young, so beautiful, so full of hope and promise, they went on lightly through the sunlight as their own happy thoughts might then be traversing the years to come and making them all years of brightness."
"So they passed away into the shadow and were gone."
That phrase — passed away — is not accidental. It carries its full weight.
It is a passage of very great beauty, and I think it is important not to over-explain it.
The cloud passing over the sun is not a symbol to be decoded. It is an atmosphere to be felt.
Dickens is giving us, I would argue, something closer to the Shakespearean premonitory image than to allegory.
What matters is the human fact behind that image: that Mr. Jarndyce, this good man, had himself once contemplated the very union now unfolding.
He tells Richard directly, with that characteristic mixture of warmth and rueful self-knowledge.
"I certainly did contemplate, afar off, the possibility of you and your pretty cousin here being in a mind to go through life together."
"But that was afar off, Rick, afar off!"
That repetition — afar off, afar off — is the gesture of a man who has relinquished something with great dignity and very little fuss.
Edmund, I think you're right that Jarndyce's restraint there is one of the finest things in the book.
But I want to press on to Chapter Seventeen, because that's where the machinery of Richard's failure becomes explicit — and in a very Dickensian way.
It's Mrs. Badger — wonderfully named — who delivers the diagnosis, and she does it with perfect social composure.
She tells Esther that Richard is, quote, languid about the profession of medicine.
That he lacks what she calls a positive interest — and then she makes the contrast that stings.

"Young men like Mr. Allan Woodcourt who take it from a strong interest in all that it can do will find some reward in it through a great deal of work for a very little money and through years of considerable endurance and disappointment."
Woodcourt, of course, is everything Richard isn't — which is why Dickens plants him here as a quiet rebuke.
What I love about Mrs. Badger is that she isn't cruel. She's thorough.
She has assessed Richard with the calm professionalism one might apply to a mildly disappointing cut of meat.
And the comic surface of that scene makes it land harder when Richard, much later, says the same thing about himself — without the composure.
Because in Chapter Twenty-Three, talking to Esther, Richard strips the comedy away entirely.
"My dear Esther, I understand you, and I wish to heaven I were a more constant sort of fellow."

"If I were a more constant sort of fellow, I should have held on either to Badger or to Kenge and Carboy like grim death, and should have begun to be steady and systematic by this time, and shouldn't be in debt, and—"
And the sentence breaks off. The dash. That dash is everything.
Oliver has put his finger on something that I think is the moral centre of Richard's tragedy.
He knows. He has always, at some level, known.
Richard is not an innocent corrupted by Chancery, as some readings have it. He is a young man of weak will who finds in Chancery a magnificent excuse.
What makes the confession to Esther so moving is that for one clear moment, before the suit swallows him again, he sees himself without the excuse.
Constant to myself — not to Ada, he's careful to say, but to himself — is the phrase that carries everything.
That is not a young man destroyed by an institution. That is a young man who has not yet become fully himself, and may not live to do so.
I'd push back just slightly on that — not on the moral reading, which is beautiful, but on the question of responsibility.
Dickens is doing something quite deliberate architecturally: he gives us Mrs. Badger's diagnosis before Richard's self-diagnosis.
The institution confirms what the character already is. That sequence matters.
Richard doesn't need Chancery to make him inconstant — but Chancery is uniquely, brilliantly designed to exploit inconstancy once it exists.
It offers perpetual deferral. It says: your real life begins when the case is settled.
And for a man who cannot commit to the present, that promise is fatal.
And all the while, Ada believes in him. That's where the pathos lives, for me, as a performer.
Go back to that image of them leaving the room — Ada looking up at Richard's face and seeming to see nothing else.
She listens, she looks up, she sees nothing else. In five words, her entire tragedy.
When I read that passage aloud — and I have read it many times — I always pause at the moment the room darkens.
"The room darkened as they went out, and the sun was clouded over."
You let that sit. You don't rush into the next thing. The silence is part of the sentence.
Three readings, three angles — and I think what's emerged is that Richard's story is both a character study and a structural argument, and Dickens refuses to let one cancel out the other.
Eleanor, Edmund, Oliver — thank you. We'll return after a short break to look at how the novel frames these personal failures against the broader world of Chancery.

segments.title: Lady Dedlock's Shadow: Secrets and Surveillance

utterances.text: Welcome back to Bleak House Unpacked.
We've spent time with the fog and the Court of Chancery, but today we turn to what I think is the novel's most psychologically charged relationship.
Lady Dedlock and Mr. Tulkinghorn — mistress and solicitor, each holding the other in a kind of cold mutual surveillance.
With me are three people who I suspect will find a great deal to disagree about here, which is exactly what I want.
Dr. Eleanor Hartley, whose fascination with narrative architecture makes her the ideal reader of Dickens's most carefully constructed scenes.
Sir Edmund Leigh, who will insist — rightly — that we keep our eyes on character and moral imagination rather than symbol.
And Oliver Trevelyan, who has read Tulkinghorn aloud more times than most people have read him on the page, and knows exactly where the silences fall.
Let's begin with the man himself — Tulkinghorn arriving at Chesney Wold just before sunset.
What I love about Tulkinghorn's arrival is that Dickens gives him no entrance — he simply appears.
There's no carriage, no announcement — just this slow, inexorable figure materialising on the terrace.
And then the prose does something extraordinary.
"He carries family secrets in every limb of his body and every crease of his dress."
Every limb. Every crease. The man is a walking archive.

And then Dickens turns the screw further — he asks whether Tulkinghorn's soul is genuinely devoted to the great families, or whether he simply sells them a service and keeps himself entirely separate.
The answer, magnificently, is that we never find out.
And notice how structurally that description mirrors Tulkinghorn's function in the plot itself.
He is opaque to us as readers in precisely the way he is opaque to Lady Dedlock.
Dickens refuses to give us privileged access to his interiority — and that refusal is the technique.
The parenthetical — "if it be a mask" — is so good I almost want to underline it.
Because it opens the possibility that there is no mask — that this expressionlessness is simply what he is.
That is far more frightening than any conventional villain.
You are both, I think, making Tulkinghorn more Gothic than he is.
What Dickens has actually drawn is a study in a particular English professional type — the man of absolute discretion who has made discretion into a form of power.
"He is his own client in that matter, and will never betray himself."
That is a portrait of a man with an entirely coherent — if chilling — moral philosophy.
He is not evil in any theatrical sense. He is simply impenetrable, and he has chosen to be so.
And it's into this impenetrable presence that Lady Dedlock now has to walk — because Sir Leicester has been given a message.
Tulkinghorn has found the man who copied the affidavit — the man whose handwriting threw Lady Dedlock into her one visible moment of crisis.
Eleanor, the scene of Sir Leicester reading that letter aloud — how does Dickens manage the tension?
It is a scene of almost unbearable dramatic irony — because Sir Leicester has absolutely no idea what he is delivering.
He fumbles with the letter, loses his place, apologises — and every fumble is agony for Lady Dedlock and for us.
The comedy of his searching — "I beg your pardon, that's not the place" — is pitch-perfect because it plays against the dread.
And then the message itself lands with extraordinary precision.
"I have something to tell her on her return in reference to the person who copied the affidavit in the Chancery suit, which so powerfully stimulated her curiosity. I have seen him."
Those last three words — "I have seen him" — are the most compressed threat in the novel.
Tulkinghorn doesn't say what he knows. He says only that he has seen. That is enough.
I've read that scene aloud many times and the thing that always catches me is the note of absolute courtesy in Tulkinghorn's message.
"Respectful compliments to my Lady, who I hope has benefited by the change." It's a health inquiry wrapped around a grenade.
And Lady Dedlock's response — she looks a little irritated at Sir Leicester's fumbling.
The reader knows exactly why. The irritation is barely-contained terror dressed as aristocratic impatience.
Dickens gives her no inner monologue. We read her through the slightest physical gesture. It is astonishing craft.
I want to say something in Lady Dedlock's defence here, which may surprise you.
Sir Leicester's final speech in this episode — his insistence that no association in my Lady's mind could possibly be traceable to this poor wretch — is, in its way, an act of love.
He is protecting her from suspicion in the only way he knows — by the exercise of rank and assumption.
It is tragically misplaced, yes. But it is not empty. He believes in her absolutely.
The novel is not kind to that belief. But Dickens at least dignifies it.
And yet the person who is not being dignified — who is being watched with minute precision — is Lady Dedlock herself.
Because when Tulkinghorn speaks to her directly, something remarkable happens between them.
Oliver — there's a passage about the way they look at each other during this conversation that I think you should read for us.
It is one of the great paragraphs in the book — and the book has several hundred contenders for that title.
Dickens tells us that throughout their short exchange, both of them have maintained their customary deportment — perfectly still on the surface.

"But whether each evermore watches and suspects the other, evermore mistrustful of some great reservation; whether each is evermore prepared at all points for the other, and never to be taken unawares; what each would give to know how much the other knows—all this is hidden, for the time, in their own hearts."
"For the time." Those two words at the end are doing everything.
Because we know — the novel has already told us — that this concealment is temporary. The reckoning is already in motion.
The rhetorical structure of that passage is extraordinary — the triple anaphora of "whether... whether... what."
Each clause is a question Dickens refuses to answer, piling uncertainty upon uncertainty.
And then the grammatical pivot — all of this is hidden — which formally enacts the concealment it describes.
The form is the meaning. The sentence withholds what it is about withholding.
I grant the rhetorical skill. But I want to stay with what is actually at stake morally.
These are two people concealing things — but their concealments are of entirely different moral weight.
Lady Dedlock conceals a past that would, if disclosed, destroy the people she loves.
Tulkinghorn conceals his intentions — and those intentions are predatory.
The novel presents them as symmetrical — both watching, both guarded — but they are not morally equivalent. Dickens knows this even when the prose pretends otherwise.
That asymmetry is beautifully put, Edmund.
Because it persists — across multiple meetings, across days and dinners at Chesney Wold.
Eleanor, how does Dickens describe this ongoing surveillance between them?
The passage is almost hypnotic in its repetition — Dickens enacts the tedium of sustained watchfulness.
They meet again at dinner — again, next day — again, for many days in succession.
"Lady Dedlock is always the same exhausted deity, surrounded by worshippers, and terribly liable to be bored to death, even while presiding at her own shrine."
Exhausted deity. It is one of the great compressed portraits in Victorian fiction.
She is worshipped and bored simultaneously — bored precisely because she is worshipped.
And the shrine image makes her predicament theological — she is trapped in a role that has become her entire prison.
And opposite her — "the same speechless repository of noble confidences, so oddly out of place and yet so perfectly at home."
There is something almost comic in that juxtaposition — and I mean comic in the darkest possible sense.
He doesn't belong there by class or manner — and yet he is the one who controls the room.
The exhausted deity is, in fact, entirely at his mercy. The repository holds all the cards.
Which brings me to the question that the novel raises rather quietly through the Esther strand — the question of what Lady Dedlock is actually protecting.
We learn through Mr. Jarndyce — from that letter, that remarkable document — that the woman who arranged Esther's upbringing had made an absolute resolution.
"That more than this she would never — and he was well persuaded of the steadfastness of her resolution — for any human consideration disclose."
For any human consideration. That is a phrase of iron will.
This is not a weak woman being hunted. This is a woman who has chosen, with absolute deliberation, the terms of her own concealment.
Tulkinghorn may stalk her. But she is not without agency in this story.
That's a crucial corrective, Edmund — and I think it changes how we read Esther's narration of that passage.
Esther hears this second-hand, through Jarndyce, relayed through Kenge — layers of mediation, each one adding distance.
And yet what cuts through all that distance is this single fact of resolution — this word steadfastness.
Lady Dedlock has sealed herself. And in sealing herself she has, without knowing it, sealed her daughter's understanding of her own origins.
The secret is not just about survival. It has become a structural fact about Esther's entire life.
Secrets as structural facts — I think that's the note we need to carry forward.
Lady Dedlock, Tulkinghorn, Esther — bound together by what cannot be said, and watched over by a narrator who sees everything but holds his tongue at precisely the right moments.
After the break, we'll turn to the other great world of this novel — the fog-bound streets of London and the people Chancery has left behind.

segments.title: Jo and the Doctrine of Indifference

utterances.text: Welcome back to Bleak House Unpacked.

I'm joined today by three remarkable readers of this novel — Dr. Eleanor Hartley, whose own fiction and whose teaching at the heart of the creative writing world gives her an eye for how Dickens builds his effects from the inside.
Sir Edmund Leigh, whose decades at Oxford have given him a patience for moral complexity and a healthy suspicion of any reading that flatters our politics at the expense of the novel.
And Oliver Trevelyan, who has read more Dickens aloud than almost anyone alive, and who hears in this prose things the rest of us can only catch when he points them out.
Today we're in the inquest chapter — the inquiry into the death of the man known only as Nemo — and we're watching Dickens work simultaneously on two frequencies.
Comic grotesque and piercing tenderness, sometimes within the same paragraph.
Eleanor, let's start with you — because there is a structural boldness in this chapter that I suspect you've been wanting to talk about.
Yes — and thank you, because the structure here is genuinely audacious.

Within this single chapter Dickens holds three registers in the air at once: legal farce, social tragedy, and what I can only call direct apostrophe — the narrator turning away from the scene entirely to address Jo personally.
That last move — the direct address — is the most startling.
The narrator suddenly steps out of the inquest room and speaks directly to this illiterate crossing-sweeper as though he is the most important person in England.
And the passage that results is extraordinary — listen to how it's phrased.
"There is something like a distant ray of light in thy muttered reason for this: 'He wos wery good to me, he wos!'"
That orthography — 'wos wery good' — is doing extraordinary double work.
It marks Jo's exclusion from formal language, and simultaneously it is the most morally luminous sentence in the chapter.
Eleanor has put her finger on precisely what defeats you when you try to read this passage aloud.
Because you have to find a voice that is simultaneously tender and angry — not performing tenderness, not performing anger, but holding both at once.
And the rhythm Dickens gives you helps.
'Jo, is it thou?' — three words, then a pause built into the question itself.
'Well, well!' — and there's the sigh, the weight of the world, before he even begins.
Then contrast that — sharply — with Mrs. Piper.
Because Mrs. Piper is the comic engine of this chapter, and she's utterly magnificent.
Dickens tells us she has a good deal to say, 'chiefly in parentheses and without punctuation, but not much to tell.'
That sentence is itself a comedy of form — the description enacts the thing it describes.
Oliver's instinct for the comedy is right, and I don't want to dampen it — but I think we should resist the temptation to treat Mrs. Piper merely as relief.
She is not simply there to make us laugh before the novel punches us again.
She represents something genuinely sinister — the community's appetite to construct a villain from a man it never troubled to know.
What I find remarkable is the contrast Dickens draws between her testimony — voluminous, parenthetical, groundless — and what Jo actually knows about the dead man.
And what Jo knows is this: one cold winter night, the man turned to look at him and came back.
"Neither have I. Not one!" and gave him the price of a supper and a night's lodging.
The shortest possible syntax — and the most devastating moral statement in the chapter.
Two men without a friend in the world, meeting by a crossing at night.
Edmund, that observation about the syntax is crucial — because Dickens has given the two speakers inverted proportions, and it's deliberate.
Mrs. Piper's testimony sprawls across an enormous run-on sentence with parentheses inside parentheses — Alexander James Piper aged eighteen months, the half-baptizing, all of it.
And Jo's testimony — the testimony the court dismisses — is spare, exact, and quietly shattering.
Notice too how Dickens describes him: 'that graceless creature only knows.'
'That graceless creature only knows' — the narrator adopts the court's contemptuous label and then proceeds to destroy it.
Because what the graceless creature knows turns out to be everything that matters.
There's a question the dead man asks Jo that stops me every single time.
Dickens tells us the man had often asked Jo 'whether he ever wished to die.'
'And similar strange questions,' the narrator adds — as if wishing to die were simply a peculiar conversational habit.
That throwaway line contains the whole biography of a man who eventually chose a room in a slum to die in, alone.
And the boy overheard all of it, understood none of it formally, and yet has preserved it faithfully.
Jo is the novel's truest witness — which is precisely why the law won't hear him.
I want to push back — gently — on the tendency to read this purely as a polemic against legal institutions.
What Dickens is doing here is older and deeper than that.
The chapter is structured around two forms of judgment — the court's, and the narrator's — and Dickens is asking which carries genuine moral authority.
The court dismisses Jo because he cannot articulate religious belief in formal terms — he 'can't exactly say' what will be done to him.
And yet the narrator — who is in some sense the novel's own tribunal — finds him 'not quite in outer darkness.'
That phrase is doing theological work, not merely sentimental work.
Dickens is arguing that natural love — a boy's gratitude for one act of kindness — constitutes a form of grace the court cannot measure and cannot extinguish.
Edmund's point about theological resonance is exactly right — and I'd add that the formal archaic register of the apostrophe reinforces it.
'Jo, is it thou?' — Dickens shifts into the second-person singular of scripture and prayer.
He doesn't address Jo as 'you' — the language of bureaucracy, of the court, of dismissal.
He addresses him as 'thou' — the language of intimacy, of the Psalms, of a human soul spoken to directly by God.
It is one of the most quietly revolutionary choices in Victorian fiction.
We've been talking about individual witnesses — Jo, Mrs. Piper, the dead man glimpsed through their eyes.
But this novel is full of characters who are witnesses to injustice and must decide whether to speak — and at what cost.
In a moment we'll turn to two of the novel's most anguished silences — and what finally breaks them.
Welcome to Bleak House Unpacked, the show that takes one of the great novels seriously — all the way down.
Today's segment asks a question that might sound simple but isn't: how does Dickens hold genuine moral weight and savage comic performance in the same novel?
Our three guests bring very different answers.
Dr. Eleanor Hartley is a novelist and creative writing teacher whose eye for the architecture of a sentence is, frankly, alarming.
Sir Edmund Leigh is a retired Oxford don who reads novels as stories about individual character tested by circumstance — and whose scepticism of fashionable readings keeps us all honest.
And Oliver Trevelyan has narrated more classic novels than almost anyone alive — he hears the prose the way a conductor hears a score.
Let's begin with Mr. Jarndyce — a man who speaks in the novel with a quality of moral seriousness that keeps surprising you.
What strikes me about Jarndyce is that Dickens gives him the hardest possible assignment: be genuinely good without being tedious.
And the way he achieves that is through a kind of rhetorical self-interruption — Jarndyce is always catching himself before he becomes the thing he wants to warn against.
There's a passage early in his counsel to Ada and Richard that demonstrates this perfectly.
He says: "I might tell you that you don't know your own minds yet, that a thousand things may happen to divert you from one another — but I will not do that."
He names the lecture he could give, and then refuses to give it — which is, of course, far more persuasive than giving it.
That is a writer who understands that goodness, rendered directly, curdles into sentimentality.
Eleanor is quite right, and I would add that what makes Jarndyce extraordinary is his refusal to exercise the power he manifestly possesses.
He tells these young people, with what I can only call studied modesty, that he has no power over them whatsoever.
But of course the very act of saying so is itself an exercise of moral authority — Dickens knows this, and Jarndyce knows this.
And then comes the address to Richard, which is — I'll say it plainly — one of the finest pieces of practical moral instruction in the English novel.
"Trust in nothing but in Providence and your own efforts. Never separate the two, like the heathen waggoner."
The heathen waggoner — that is a scholar's allusion made perfectly colloquial.
It is the voice of a man who has read his Aesop and his Scripture and understood them both as practical guidance rather than ornament.
Edmund, I agree entirely about that passage — and as someone who has actually spoken those lines aloud for a recording, I can tell you the rhythm is extraordinary.
"Constancy in love is a good thing, but it means nothing, and is nothing, without constancy in every kind of effort."
The repetition of 'nothing' — twice, almost casually — that is a performer's gift from the author.
But now — can we talk about Vholes?
Because Vholes is the other side of this coin entirely — and he is one of the great comic monsters in all of Dickens.
Here is a man who delivers devastating professional verdicts and then pivots, in a single breath, to polite social pleasantry.

"I openly say, unpalatable as it may be, that I consider Mr. C.'s affairs in a very bad way, that I consider Mr. C. himself in a very bad way, and that I regard this as an exceedingly ill-advised marriage."
And then immediately: "Am I here, sir? Yes, I thank you — enjoying the pleasure of some agreeable conversation with Miss Summerson!"
The audacity of that transition — I genuinely laugh every time.
What makes Vholes so effective, structurally, is that Dickens anchors him in this almost parodic professionalism.
He notes his own words in his diary — which he then makes a point of mentioning he noted them — so that everything he does is traceable, attributable, charged to someone.
Except — and this is the sting — he adds that his present candour "can be charged to no one."
"I regard it in the light of a professional duty to be so, though it can be charged to no one."
The generosity is weaponised — and the victim can't even bill anyone for the wound.
I confess Vholes makes me slightly uneasy — precisely because he is so entertaining.
The comic grotesque has a tendency to displace moral judgement rather than invite it.
We laugh at Vholes — but the man is destroying Richard Carstone, who is not, beneath his weakness and his vanity, an unsympathetic figure.

Jarndyce's warning to Richard — "if you entertain the supposition that any real success ever was or could be wrested from Fortune by fits and starts, leave that wrong idea here" — that warning is Richard's entire tragedy compressed.
The comedy around Vholes is real, but it should make us wince, not merely chuckle.
Edmund, I take your point entirely — and I think the Smallweed scene is where Dickens makes you feel both registers simultaneously, without flinching from either.
There is Mr. Bucket, whispering about the Smallweed family's spectacular capacity for betrayal.
"There ain't one of the family that wouldn't sell the other for a pound or two, except the old lady — and she's only out of it because she's too weak in her mind to drive a bargain."
Now — on one level that is a magnificent joke.

But Edmund's point holds: in the background of that joke is a burnt, stained will — a document that could have changed everything — retrieved from people too busy betraying each other to profit from it.
The comedy and the catastrophe are the same fact, seen from different angles.
That phrase — "with the dexterity of a conjuror" — is doing a lot of work in that scene.
Bucket transfers that document in an instant — a life's litigation, a family's ruin — as if it were a card trick.
And Dickens names it as conjuring, which is both delightful and terrible — because in the Chancery world, justice and sleight of hand are not always distinguishable.
The comic mirror — and I think that image holds — shows us characters who are funny precisely because the systems around them are so badly broken.
Vholes, Smallweed, Bucket with his conjuror's hands — they're all reflections of Chancery's moral distortions, rendered in brilliant caricature.
And against all that, Jarndyce stands offering something radical in this novel's world: plain, undeceiving goodness.
We'll be back after the break to look at how Dickens handles what lies beneath all that comedy — in the silences, and the suffering, and the deaths.
Welcome back to Bleak House Unpacked, the programme where we take our time with a novel that rewards every minute you give it.
Today we're turning to one of the novel's great preoccupations: who holds power, and who is crushed by the lack of it.
Dickens gives us figures from the most glamorous heights of society to its most invisible depths — and he insists we look at all of them.
With me today are three readers whose perspectives, taken together, I think will do justice to the range of this novel.
Dr. Eleanor Hartley teaches creative writing and thinks hard about how novelists build their effects from the ground up — sentence by sentence, image by image.
Sir Edmund Leigh is a retired Oxford don who reads novels as moral investigations — stories about character, conscience, and what human beings are capable of.
And Oliver Trevelyan has read more classic novels aloud than perhaps anyone alive — he hears the rhythms of the prose in a way the rest of us can only aspire to.
Edmund, I'd like to start with you — because Dickens opens this territory with something that might seem like a digression about fashion, but is in fact something far more pointed.
Indeed, and I think it is one of the most brilliantly constructed comic reversals in the novel.
Lady Dedlock supposes herself to be, in the narrator's marvellous phrase, an inscrutable Being — quite beyond the comprehension of ordinary mortals.
And yet every tradesman who serves her — every dim little star revolving about her — has taken the most precise measure of her weaknesses.
Dickens gives us the image of these apparently subservient people who are in reality the puppet-masters.
The passage builds to a simile of extraordinary reach — listen to this.
"who, in hooking one, hook all and bear them off as Lemuel Gulliver bore away the stately fleet of the majestic Lilliput"
The aristocracy, that stately fleet — borne off by tradespeople who affect to prostrate themselves before it.
It is satirical, yes — but it is not merely satirical. It is a precise observation about the nature of deference and power.
What strikes me about that passage is the architectural cunning of it.
Dickens gives the tradespeople their own voices — Blaze and Sparkle, Sheen and Gloss, Mr. Sladdery — in direct speech, each one explaining exactly how the manipulation works.
And Mr. Sladdery's refrain — "my high connexion, sir" repeated four times in a single breath — that's comic writing of the highest order.
But the real structural move is the narrator's final aside — that Mr. Sladdery, who is an honest man, does not exaggerate at all.
The honesty of the tradesman is precisely what makes the satire devastating. He is not cynical. He is merely accurate.
Sheen and Gloss! You couldn't improve on those names with an hour and a dictionary.
When I read Sladdery aloud, I find that repeated "sir" is everything — it's the dagger concealed in the bow.
But Edmund's right that the Gulliver image is the crown of the passage. That word "stately" — applied to Lady Dedlock's set — carries a whole fleet of irony within it.
And then Dickens pulls the rug: these grand Lilliputs think they command the sea. In fact they are being sailed away.
From the drawing rooms of the great, the novel descends — and the descent is sheer.
In the tenth chapter, Tulkinghorn enters a room in which lies a man known only as Nemo — nobody.
Dickens's description of that room and that body is among the most clinically gothic passages he ever wrote.
The candle has guttered so low that its wick has doubled over — a tower of winding-sheet above it.
The metaphor of the shroud is already in the room before we understand the man is dead or dying.
And then Dickens delivers this — and I think it is one of the great sentences of the novel.
"through the general sickliness and faintness, and the odour of stale tobacco, there comes into the lawyer's mouth the bitter, vapid taste of opium"
It enters through the mouth. The lawyer tastes the room. We taste it with him.
That sentence is extraordinary for what it does with point of view.
We are suddenly locked inside Tulkinghorn's body — his mouth — at the very moment he perceives something he does not yet understand.
It's a technique that slows time to the pace of a breath. We know before Tulkinghorn knows, and we know it through sensation.
"Bitter" and "vapid" together — one word for taste, one for emptiness. Dickens is describing a life as much as a drug.
When I read that passage aloud, I find myself slowing almost to a stop on the word "vapid."
Because there is something in that word — flat, stale, empty — that carries Nemo's entire existence.
The room is foul. The air is foul. And yet Dickens won't let you simply recoil — he makes the lawyer taste it, and therefore makes you taste it.
That's the moral trick of the novel, isn't it? You cannot stand outside this world and observe it safely. You are put inside it.
Oliver touches on something I think is central to the novel's moral project — the refusal of comfortable distance.
Nowhere is this more concentrated than in the testimony of the boy Jo — a passage of perhaps twelve lines that has never left me.
Dickens strips language itself down. Jo does not know his surname. He does not know that names have two parts.
And then comes the passage I find almost unbearable in its plainness.
"No father, no mother, no friends. Never been to school."
Four phrases. No verbs. Each one a closed door.
And yet Jo is not without moral knowledge. He knows a broom is a broom. He knows it is wicked to tell a lie.
He cannot say who taught him — he simply knows. The novel asks what that knowledge costs him and what society owes him for possessing it.
I have read Jo's testimony aloud more times than I can count, and it never becomes routine.
The capitalisations — "HE don't find no fault with it" — tell you Dickens is mimicking a voice giving evidence, halting, one syllable at a time.
What staggers me is the sentence about punishment after death — Jo believes something bad will happen to him if he lies to the gentlemen, and so he'll tell the truth.
He has absorbed conscience without catechism. He has morality without institution. That is the novel's most devastating indictment of its world.
The grammar of that passage is doing everything. Dickens is using sentence fragments as a structural argument.
Each truncated phrase enacts Jo's truncated existence — no subject, no object, no future tense.
And then Edmund's point about the moral knowledge — Dickens lets Jo have that. It's the one thing the system couldn't strip from him.
Which makes the indifference of Chancery — that great grinding machine — all the more monstrous when we encounter it in the next figure: Gridley.
Gridley is, to my mind, one of the novel's most harrowing studies in the destruction of a man by a system.
He is introduced as a standing joke — the man from Shropshire — a figure of fun in the Court of Chancery.
Five and twenty years of legal proceedings have reduced a man to a punchline. And he knows it.
His self-declaration — and it is a declaration, almost a formal claim — runs as follows.
"I am the man from Shropshire. I have been dragged for five and twenty years over burning iron, and I have lost the habit of treading upon velvet."
Burning iron and velvet — the two surfaces of English life in this novel — and Gridley can no longer walk on one of them.
He beats one hand against the other as he speaks — the gesture of a man hammering at a wall that will never give way.
"Burning iron" — I always feel that image in my feet. That is the mark of a great metaphor: it inhabits the body.
And the repetition — "I am the man from Shropshire" — said after explaining it is a joke against him.
He reclaims the insult. He turns the joke back into a name — his name, the only one that matters now.
There's a terrible dignity in that. And performing it, you feel it — you feel the exact weight of twenty-five years in those four words.
What links Gridley to Jo, and to Nemo, is that Dickens gives each of them a kind of residual selfhood that the system has failed to erase.
Nemo has collapsed into anonymity, but he had a life — we feel its ghost in that room.
Jo has been given nothing, but he has kept something no one taught him and no one can take.
And Gridley has been ground down to a single identity — the man from Shropshire — and he wears it like armour.
The system may define you. But Dickens insists that it does not entirely constitute you. That is what makes the novel something more than protest.
Edmund, Eleanor, Oliver — that is a set of readings I think listeners will want to sit with for a while.
From the gilded manipulation of Lady Dedlock's world to Jo's four wordless closed doors — the novel's range is extraordinary.
What unites all these figures, as Eleanor says, is that Dickens never lets the system have the last word on any human being.
We'll return after the break to look further into the novel's architecture — and into some of the characters who navigate these worlds with rather more cunning than the system expects.

segments.title: Dickens's Double Vision: Narration and Truth

utterances.text: We've spent this episode navigating the extraordinary architecture of Bleak House — its two narrators, its fog, its law, its secrets.
And in this final segment, I want to bring us to a question that has been hovering over everything we've said: what does Dickens himself believe about truth?
Not legal truth, not social truth — but the truth a novel can tell about human beings under pressure.
Eleanor, Edmund, Oliver — let's see if we can bring this enormous book to something like a resting point.
I want to start, if I may, with Boythorn — because I think he's one of Dickens's great gifts to us, and he's been criminally underappreciated today.
Here is a man conducting a private war against the aristocracy with a fire engine and some split peas, and doing it with the absolute conviction of the righteous.
Dickens gives him this magnificent tirade, and it builds and builds until you get the only possible ending for such a speech.
"He brings actions for trespass; I bring actions for trespass. He brings actions for assault and battery; I defend them and continue to assault and batter. Ha, ha, ha!"
That laughter at the end — those three 'Ha's — they're not written, they're performed. They're stage directions built into prose.
And the thing about Boythorn is that Dickens loves him completely — the excess, the absurdity, the sheer operatic fury of him.
But he also means him. Boythorn is right. Sir Leicester is precisely the stiff-necked imbecile he describes.
Oliver's absolutely right that the comedy is doing serious work — but I want to set Boythorn against Tulkinghorn, because that contrast is where Dickens's double vision becomes most acute.
Boythorn rages openly, theatrically, in full daylight. Tulkinghorn operates in shadow, and his power is precisely the power of withholding.
There's a moment in chapter forty-one where Tulkinghorn speaks to Lady Dedlock about his own leverage over her — and the language is extraordinary.
"I would as soon have hoped to root up by means of my own strength and my own hands the oldest tree on this estate as to shake your hold upon Sir Leicester."
He is telling her: your position was unassailable. And yet I found the means. The sentence enacts the slow, rooting violence of what he's done to her.
Structurally, the image of the oldest tree on the estate does something Dickens does all through this novel — it smuggles the estate itself into the metaphor.
Chesney Wold is not just the setting. It is the condition of the Dedlocks' existence — and Tulkinghorn has found the root.
What strikes me — and I think this is where Dickens transcends the satirist — is the moment when the comedy and the gothic fall silent together.
Late in the novel, George Rouncewell walks through Chesney Wold at night. He is holding a lamp at arm's length through those grand empty rooms.
He is thinking of the murdered Tulkinghorn, of the vanished Lady Dedlock, of Sir Leicester broken upstairs. And the prose arrives at this.
"He MIGHT see something now, which it would tax his boldness to walk up to, lay his hand upon, and prove to be a fancy. But it is all blank, blank as the darkness above and below."
That word 'blank' falling twice — it is not mere atmosphere. It is the moral verdict on everything that pride and secrecy and legal manoeuvre have produced.
Boythorn's laughter, Tulkinghorn's cold leverage, Lady Dedlock's secret — all of it ends here, in rooms that answer no questions and give nothing back.
Dickens, for all his energy and comedy, is finally a tragic writer. I think we must admit that.
I wouldn't quarrel with that — though I'd say he is a comic writer and a tragic writer simultaneously, sometimes in the same paragraph.
What Edmund has described in that George passage — that quality of blankness, the house refusing to confess — is exactly what makes the novel so difficult to shake off.
You finish Bleak House and the fog hasn't entirely cleared. That's intentional. Dickens leaves the question open.
And that — I think — is what separates a great novel from a very good one. The great one continues to ask you questions after you've put it down.
What I keep returning to is the double narration — Esther's warmth and the omniscient narrator's cold irony — and how Dickens uses that formal architecture as a kind of stereo vision.
Esther cannot see Tulkinghorn's scene with Lady Dedlock. The omniscient narrator can, and renders it in that chilling, deliberate prose.
Between them, Dickens constructs a world that no single witness could have reported truly.
That is the double vision of the title of this segment — and it is, I think, one of the great formal achievements in the English novel.
I find myself in unexpected agreement with Eleanor — though I would put it rather differently.
What the two narrators together achieve is the demonstration that moral truth and social fact are not the same thing — and that literature is the only instrument delicate enough to hold both at once.
Esther gives us goodness. The omniscient narrator gives us reality. The novel insists we need both.
Goodness and reality. I can't think of a better place to leave it.
Eleanor Hartley, Edmund Leigh, Oliver Trevelyan — this has been a genuine pleasure, and I think listeners will want to go straight back to the novel after this conversation.
Bleak House, published in monthly parts between 1852 and 1853, remains one of the greatest and most demanding novels in the English language.
We hope this episode has made it a little less bleak — and a great deal more alive.
Thank you for listening to Bleak House Unpacked.

slept sound at night, and how he bore cold and hunger, and whether he
ever wished to die, and similar strange questions. That when the man

c13:p115.text:
“Well!” said Mr. Jarndyce. “That’s rational. Now, hear me, my dears!
I might tell you that you don’t know your own minds yet, that a
thousand things may happen to divert you from one another, that it is
well this chain of flowers you have taken up is very easily broken,
or it might become a chain of lead. But I will not do that. Such
wisdom will come soon enough, I dare say, if it is to come at all. I
will assume that a few years hence you will be in your hearts to one
another what you are to-day. All I say before speaking to you
according to that assumption is, if you DO change—if you DO come to
find that you are more commonplace cousins to each other as man and
woman than you were as boy and girl (your manhood will excuse me,
Rick!)—don’t be ashamed still to confide in me, for there will be
nothing monstrous or uncommon in it. I am only your friend and
distant kinsman. I have no power over you whatever. But I wish and
hope to retain your confidence if I do nothing to forfeit it.”

c13:p118.text:
“Come!” said Mr. Jarndyce. “Now for our assumption. Now we lift our
eyes up and look hopefully at the distance! Rick, the world is before
you; and it is most probable that as you enter it, so it will receive
you. Trust in nothing but in Providence and your own efforts. Never
separate the two, like the heathen waggoner. Constancy in love is a
good thing, but it means nothing, and is nothing, without constancy
in every kind of effort. If you had the abilities of all the great
men, past and present, you could do nothing well without sincerely
meaning it and setting about it. If you entertain the supposition
that any real success, in great things or in small, ever was or could
be, ever will or can be, wrested from Fortune by fits and starts,
leave that wrong idea here or leave your cousin Ada here.”

words, for I happened afterwards to note them in my diary, which is
producible at any time—I mentioned to you that Mr. C. had laid down

of mine laid down a principle which was not of an immoral (that is to
say, unlawful) nature, it devolved upon me to carry it out. I HAVE
carried it out; I do carry it out. But I will not smooth things over
to any connexion of Mr. C.’s on any account. As open as I was to Mr.
Jarndyce, I am to you. I regard it in the light of a professional
duty to be so, though it can be charged to no one. I openly say,
unpalatable as it may be, that I consider Mr. C.’s affairs in a very
bad way, that I consider Mr. C. himself in a very bad way, and that I
regard this as an exceedingly ill-advised marriage. Am I here, sir?
Yes, I thank you; I am here, Mr. C., and enjoying the pleasure of
some agreeable conversation with Miss Summerson, for which I have to

Having given us one glance out of the watching corner of his eye, and
having given his nose one triumphant rub with his forefinger, Mr.
Bucket stood with his eyes fastened on his confidential friend and
his hand stretched forth ready to take the paper and present it to my
guardian. It was not produced without much reluctance and many
declarations on the part of Mr. Smallweed that he was a poor
industrious man and that he left it to Mr. Jarndyce’s honour not to
let him lose by his honesty. Little by little he very slowly took
from a breast-pocket a stained, discoloured paper which was much
singed upon the outside and a little burnt at the edges, as if it had
long ago been thrown upon a fire and hastily snatched off again. Mr.
Bucket lost no time in transferring this paper, with the dexterity of
a conjuror, from Mr. Smallweed to Mr. Jarndyce. As he gave it to my
guardian, he whispered behind his fingers, “Hadn’t settled how to
make their market of it. Quarrelled and hinted about it. I laid out
twenty pound upon it. First the avaricious grandchildren split upon
him on account of their objections to his living so unreasonably
long, and then they split on one another. Lord! There ain’t one of
the family that wouldn’t sell the other for a pound or two, except
the old lady—and she’s only out of it because she’s too weak in her
mind to drive a bargain.”

c2:p12.text:
Has Mr. Tulkinghorn any idea of this himself? It may be so, or it may
not, but there is this remarkable circumstance to be noted in
everything associated with my Lady Dedlock as one of a class—as one
of the leaders and representatives of her little world. She supposes
herself to be an inscrutable Being, quite out of the reach and ken of
ordinary mortals—seeing herself in her glass, where indeed she looks
so. Yet every dim little star revolving about her, from her maid to
the manager of the Italian Opera, knows her weaknesses, prejudices,
follies, haughtinesses, and caprices and lives upon as accurate a
calculation and as nice a measure of her moral nature as her
dressmaker takes of her physical proportions. Is a new dress, a new
custom, a new singer, a new dancer, a new form of jewellery, a new
dwarf or giant, a new chapel, a new anything, to be set up? There are
deferential people in a dozen callings whom my Lady Dedlock suspects
of nothing but prostration before her, who can tell you how to manage
her as if she were a baby, who do nothing but nurse her all their
lives, who, humbly affecting to follow with profound subservience,
lead her and her whole troop after them; who, in hooking one, hook
all and bear them off as Lemuel Gulliver bore away the stately fleet
of the majestic Lilliput. “If you want to address our people, sir,”
say Blaze and Sparkle, the jewellers—meaning by our people Lady
Dedlock and the rest—“you must remember that you are not dealing
with the general public; you must hit our people in their weakest
place, and their weakest place is such a place.” “To make this
article go down, gentlemen,” say Sheen and Gloss, the mercers, to
their friends the manufacturers, “you must come to us, because we
know where to have the fashionable people, and we can make it
fashionable.” “If you want to get this print upon the tables of my
high connexion, sir,” says Mr. Sladdery, the librarian, “or if you
want to get this dwarf or giant into the houses of my high connexion,
sir, or if you want to secure to this entertainment the patronage of
my high connexion, sir, you must leave it, if you please, to me, for
I have been accustomed to study the leaders of my high connexion,
sir, and I may tell you without vanity that I can turn them round my
finger”—in which Mr. Sladdery, who is an honest man, does not
exaggerate at all.
c2:p12.summary: Despite believing herself inscrutable, Lady Dedlock is perfectly understood and managed by tradespeople and servants who deliberately lead her and her circle by flattery and careful study of her preferences.
c2:p12.best_quote: who, in hooking one, hook all and bear them off as Lemuel Gulliver bore away the stately fleet of the majestic Lilliput

c10:p66.text:
For, on a low bed opposite the fire, a confusion of dirty patchwork,
lean-ribbed ticking, and coarse sacking, the lawyer, hesitating just
within the doorway, sees a man. He lies there, dressed in shirt and
trousers, with bare feet. He has a yellow look in the spectral
darkness of a candle that has guttered down until the whole length of
its wick (still burning) has doubled over and left a tower of
winding-sheet above it. His hair is ragged, mingling with his
whiskers and his beard—the latter, ragged too, and grown, like the
scum and mist around him, in neglect. Foul and filthy as the room is,
foul and filthy as the air is, it is not easy to perceive what fumes
those are which most oppress the senses in it; but through the
general sickliness and faintness, and the odour of stale tobacco,
there comes into the lawyer’s mouth the bitter, vapid taste of opium.

c15:p105.text:
“To your sorrow?” said the man, pausing in his wrath, “if so, I beg

into the Court of Chancery yonder and ask what is one of the standing

c9:p49.text:
“By my soul,” exclaimed Mr. Boythorn, suddenly firing another volley,
“that fellow is, and his father was, and his grandfather was, the
most stiff-necked, arrogant imbecile, pig-headed numskull, ever, by
some inexplicable mistake of Nature, born in any station of life but
a walking-stick’s! The whole of that family are the most solemnly
conceited and consummate blockheads! But it’s no matter; he should
not shut up my path if he were fifty baronets melted into one and
living in a hundred Chesney Wolds, one within another, like the ivory
balls in a Chinese carving. The fellow, by his agent, or secretary,
or somebody, writes to me ‘Sir Leicester Dedlock, Baronet, presents
his compliments to Mr. Lawrence Boythorn, and has to call his
attention to the fact that the green pathway by the old
parsonage-house, now the property of Mr. Lawrence Boythorn, is Sir
Leicester’s right of way, being in fact a portion of the park of
Chesney Wold, and that Sir Leicester finds it convenient to close up
the same.’ I write to the fellow, ‘Mr. Lawrence Boythorn presents his
compliments to Sir Leicester Dedlock, Baronet, and has to call HIS
attention to the fact that he totally denies the whole of Sir
Leicester Dedlock’s positions on every possible subject and has to
add, in reference to closing up the pathway, that he will be glad to
see the man who may undertake to do it.’ The fellow sends a most
abandoned villain with one eye to construct a gateway. I play upon
that execrable scoundrel with a fire-engine until the breath is
nearly driven out of his body. The fellow erects a gate in the night.
I chop it down and burn it in the morning. He sends his myrmidons to
come over the fence and pass and repass. I catch them in humane man
traps, fire split peas at their legs, play upon them with the
engine—resolve to free mankind from the insupportable burden of the
existence of those lurking ruffians. He brings actions for trespass;
I bring actions for trespass. He brings actions for assault and
battery; I defend them and continue to assault and batter. Ha, ha,
ha!”
c9:p49.summary: Boythorn launches an elaborate account of his escalating disputes with Sir Leicester over a right of way, detailing the volleys of letters, his theatrical retaliation with a fire engine, his destruction of gates, and the counter-actions in law, all recounted with relish and concluding with triumphant laughter.

c58:p98.text:
The trooper, his old recollections awakened by the solitary grandeur
of a great house—no novelty to him once at Chesney Wold—goes up the
stairs and through the chief rooms, holding up his light at arm’s
length. Thinking of his varied fortunes within the last few weeks,
and of his rustic boyhood, and of the two periods of his life so
strangely brought together across the wide intermediate space;
thinking of the murdered man whose image is fresh in his mind;
thinking of the lady who has disappeared from these very rooms and
the tokens of whose recent presence are all here; thinking of the
master of the house upstairs and of the foreboding, “Who will tell
him!” he looks here and looks there, and reflects how he MIGHT see
something now, which it would tax his boldness to walk up to, lay his
hand upon, and prove to be a fancy. But it is all blank, blank as the
darkness above and below, while he goes up the great staircase again,
blank as the oppressive silence.
c58:p98.summary: George patrols the grand house, his memories of past and present mingling, sensing the shadows of the missing Lady Dedlock and the murdered Tulkinghorn, finding only emptiness.
